output.impression: Tests were administered in English, his dominant language, using norms adjusted for age, education and, where available, for Spanish-English bilingual speakers; fluency and naming scores are interpreted with caution because bilingual speakers can score lower on these measures. Neuropsychological evaluation reveals a multi-domain profile with prominent amnestic and language features. Verbal memory is impaired: RAVLT delayed recall 5th percentile, immediate recall 15th percentile. Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 18th percentile), semantic fluency (Category Fluency Animals, 15th percentile) and phonemic fluency (FAS, 22nd percentile) are mildly impaired. Set-shifting is impaired (Trail Making B, 15th percentile). Visuoconstruction (Rey Complex Figure copy, 40th percentile) and simple processing speed (Trail Making A, 28th percentile) are preserved. Screening: MoCA 21/30, MMSE 26/30. Geriatric Depression Scale 6/15 (borderline). The profile is consistent with amnestic multi-domain mild cognitive impairment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 26/30 with delayed recall 1/3 not improved by cues, informant-confirmed decline over twelve months, and preserved instrumental independence, staging the syndrome as mild cognitive impairment
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: Bedside testing with cueing and his wife's account of his finances, schedule and driving decide whether he has mild cognitive impairment or dementia [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic multi-domain profile: impaired verbal delayed recall with milder naming, fluency and set-shifting deficits, interpreted with caution for a bilingual speaker
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing, interpreted with norms appropriate for his language, education and culture, to characterize the cognitive profile and set a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing defines the amnestic profile and the second domain; in a bilingual man with high-school education, naming and fluency must be read against appropriate norms [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TSH, folate, syphilis and HIV serology normal; B12 299 pg/mL low-normal; HbA1c 6.5%
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid disease, B12 deficiency (twelve years of metformin), syphilis and metabolic factors must be excluded or addressed before the decline is attributed to neurodegeneration [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Methylmalonic acid 0.26 umol/L, normal: no functional deficiency
action_criteria.label: Measure methylmalonic acid to resolve the low-normal vitamin B12
action_criteria.rationale: A serum B12 of 299 pg/mL is indeterminate in a man on long-term metformin with reduced vibration sense at the toes; a normal methylmalonic acid excludes functional deficiency [BSH_B12_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild bilateral hippocampal atrophy (MTA 1-2) with subtle temporoparietal volume loss, Fazekas 2 white matter disease and a chronic putaminal lacune
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
action_criteria.rationale: MRI shows the medial temporal atrophy that supports a neurodegenerative cause, quantifies the small vessel disease of his diabetes and hypertension, and excludes a mass, hydrocephalus or post-traumatic lesion [NIA_AA_2011] [STRIVE_2013].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity without established tau pathology: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio (0.053) with p-tau181 and total tau high-normal, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine as routine treatment for mild cognitive impairment; neither is approved for MCI and the guideline does not support routine use [AAN_dementia_2018].

Do not add an antimuscarinic bladder drug (e.g. oxybutynin) for his nocturia; anticholinergic burden worsens cognition, and tamsulosin, an alpha-1 blocker without anticholinergic effect, can continue [Beers_2023].

Do not attribute the decline to sleep apnea, poor sleep or normal aging alone, as the patient does; the amnestic multi-domain profile with hippocampal atrophy needs follow-up as mild cognitive impairment.
required_recommendations: Disclose amnestic multi-domain mild cognitive impairment with suspected Alzheimer disease pathology and a vascular contribution to the patient and his wife, explaining that it is not dementia, the risk of progression, and the value of advance planning while he has full capacity [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].

Arrange cognitive and functional reassessment in 6 to 12 months and recommend regular exercise (at least twice weekly); explain that no medicine is approved for mild cognitive impairment [AAN_dementia_2018].

Manage vascular risk factors: blood pressure is above target in clinic (153/84 mmHg) and needs review of his antihypertensive regimen, continue glycaemic control (HbA1c 6.5%) and statin therapy, and address CPAP non-adherence for his sleep apnea [AAN_dementia_2018].

Review safety with the patient and his wife: driving (hesitation at familiar intersections) at each visit, and automatic payments or a shared check of the credit card accounts after the late payments [AAN_dementia_2018].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

accepted: Amnestic multidomain mild cognitive impairment, suspected Alzheimer disease pathology (intermediate likelihood) with vascular contribution
mild cognitive impairment due to alzheimer

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / vascular contribution to dementia
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 small vessel disease, a putaminal lacune, diabetes and hypertension make a vascular contribution likely; the gradual amnestic-predominant course with hippocampal atrophy, and a decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio when tested, argue against pure vascular cognitive impairment
No visual hallucinations, no parkinsonism, no REM sleep behavior disorder, no cognitive fluctuations described
No early personality change, disinhibition, or executive-predominant profile; memory is the dominant deficit, atypical for bvFTD
GDS 6/15 is borderline and he admits frustration, but he denies persistent low mood, and recall that does not improve with cues is not typical of depression-related cognitive impairment

differential.diagnosis: Reversible cognitive impairment from thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, or untreated sleep apnea
differential.key_features: TSH 2.9 mIU/L, folate normal, B12 299 pg/mL with normal methylmalonic acid (0.26 umol/L) and homocysteine (12.3 umol/L); untreated mild OSA and nocturia fragment his sleep and may contribute, but do not explain a progressive amnestic multi-domain decline

key_clinical_evidence: Impaired delayed recall that does not improve with cueing points to a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit, the typical amnestic presentation of Alzheimer pathology [NIA_AA_MCI_2011].
In bilingual patients, naming and verbal fluency should be interpreted with language-, education- and culture-appropriate norms; lower scores on these measures alone do not establish a deficit.
A low-normal B12 in a patient on long-term metformin is indeterminate and should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before B12 deficiency is dismissed as a contributor [BSH_B12_2014].

Cholinesterase inhibitors are not approved for mild cognitive impairment and are not recommended routinely at this stage; serial assessment and vascular risk management are the evidence-based steps [AAN_dementia_2018].

Vascular risk factors and white matter disease frequently coexist with Alzheimer pathology in older adults

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Matthew Sullivan is a 66-year-old right-handed bilingual retired bus driver who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife, Maria, for evaluation of memory concerns that have been gradually worsening over the past twelve months. His wife reports that she first became concerned approximately a year ago when her husband began misplacing his keys and wallet several times a week, whereas he previously kept them in the same place consistently. She also noticed that during family gatherings, he would occasionally repeat a story he had told earlier in the same evening, apparently without realizing it. Over the past six months, he has had increasing difficulty coming up with specific words during conversation, sometimes substituting vague phrases like 'that thing' or pausing mid-sentence to search for the right term. He has begun relying heavily on his phone's calendar for appointments, whereas he previously managed his schedule from memory. His wife reports that he still manages the household finances, though she recently discovered two late credit card payments, which was unusual for him. He continues to drive locally without incident, but his wife has noticed he occasionally hesitates at familiar intersections. He still enjoys watching baseball on television and can follow game statistics, though his wife thinks he has less interest in reading the newspaper than he used to. He prepares simple meals for himself without difficulty. He has not gotten lost or had any episodes of acute confusion. There have been no personality changes, hallucinations, or behavioral disturbances. His sleep has been fragmented, partly attributed to nocturia from his prostate condition and inconsistent CPAP use. He denies persistent depressed mood but admits to some frustration about his memory. He was previously evaluated by his primary care physician six months ago, who checked basic labs and reassured him, but his wife insisted on a specialist referral because his brother has also been experiencing similar memory issues. The patient himself feels that his memory is 'not what it used to be' but believes it is a normal part of aging and that his wife is being overly worried.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Mild background diabetic retinopathy noted on fundoscopy. Facial sensation and strength symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base and stride length. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. No shuffling or festination.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and year; unable to give the exact date (states the correct month but wrong day). MMSE 26/30, losing points on delayed recall (1/3 at 5 minutes, did not improve with cues), and one point lost on serial sevens. Conversational speech is fluent but with occasional pauses for word-finding. He substitutes 'the thing you write with' for 'pen' during confrontation naming. Clock drawing is grossly intact but minute hand placement is slightly imprecise. Able to follow three-step commands. Judgment appears intact on bedside assessment. Insight is partially preserved; he acknowledges some forgetfulness but attributes it to aging and poor sleep.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. No rigidity or cogwheeling. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor or involuntary movements.

neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch and pinprick in all extremities. Vibration sense mildly reduced at bilateral great toes, likely related to peripheral neuropathy. Proprioception intact at great toes.
